text: I have a few reasons I'm worried about companies like Anthropic. The first is that our current power grid isn't sufficient for the projected needs of AI. Forget water- most of the water used by the AI is used by the power plant, so really, it's just a proxy for electricity. There's lots of ways this worry can be addressed- newer training methods that use less power, new chips that use less power, long-term building new power generation (hopefully low or no carbon). But the people with the money need to actually acknowledge the problem and look to ways to solve it. The second is the impact on jobs. This is personal, as while I'm pretty sure my own job is safe, lots of people around me aren't. And just because I'm pretty sure, doesn't mean I'm 100% sure I'm safe either. Sure, technology has always caused jobs to change- I'm not different from a buggy whip manufacturer when the automobile came out. I think a lot of people feel this way, from artists to programmers to taxi/uber drivers. Sure, new technology does this all the time, but the sheer scale and speed of what AI can do means we're impacting more jobs than ever, on a much shorter time scale. A lot of people are scared. I don't think we need to stop all AI work or anything like that- but we need to understand and address the various second and third order effects that AI is going to have, and we need thoughtful plans to address it. And for the record- if any AI companies fails, I hope it's OpenAI. Anthropic is pretty mild in comparison, in my world view. :-)

text: Show HN: Perch by mxRaven, a self-hosted mailbox and CLI in 1 file Hi HN, I have been working on mxRaven: https://mxraven.com for the past couple of months, and it has been hard to explain the idea without actually showcasing a functional use case, hence I decided to build perch. Perch is a single binary Go program that can serve IMAP + SMTP as a complete mailbox service and has an agent-friendly CLI to access and manage emails. Note that perch is open source under the MIT-0 license but it requires mxRaven to handle the public edge. However, the CLI (the `perch mail` command) can be used against any generic IMAP or SMTP submission servers (which are not necessarily perch). You can try out perch without signing up for mxRaven at https://tryperch.mxraven.com and can sign up for a free account with monthly 1k inbound + 1k outbound emails without a card. The agent-friendly CLI was not an afterthought, since LLMs have been trained heavily for utilizing POSIX-compatible shell tools for various benchmarks, I believe agents are unbelievably good when you give them tools in the language they understand: CLI. Perch can run on an old workstation in your homelab behind CGNAT or firewalls as it pulls mail in real-time from mxRaven's notification stream over a websocket. It also doesn't need to run 24*7, it can come online atleast once a day to pull the emails from mxRaven. mxRaven will not retain emails that are older than 48 hours as per our privacy policy, and it will not serve them to the pull-based consumer beyond 24 hours. The hardest part about self-hosting email is the public edge, which requires managing IP reputation, throttles and a convoluted set of authentication protocols (DKIM, SPF, DMARC, ARC etc.) and mxRaven handles that. Note that we also made a Show HN post for mxRaven itself here: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50338055 tldr, for those who don't want to read that: think of mxRaven as the WAF + router for your emails, while your applications can sit on the driver's seat for the email highway.

text: Show HN: I created a library for correctly using SQLite in Go programs Using SQLite in Go is deceptively easy. If you just import the popular github.com/mattn/go-sqlite3 as the database/sql driver implementation and start making queries, things will work great until you start hitting SQLITE_BUSY errors as traffic increases. Then you go down the same path of many gophers before you, finding GitHub and forum posts providing conflicting information on best practices for pragma values and connection handling. So I created https://github.com/cattlecloud/litesql Which provides a nice abstraction, making it easy to accidentally do the right things when using SQLite in your Go program. In particular it pools connections for read transactions and isolates a dedicated write connection for writes. It also sets pragma values to much more reasonable defaults, like isolation levels, foreign keys, cache sizes, etc. On top it provides a nice abstraction for creating periodic snapshots with retention policies. There is also litesqltest for one-line test database creation in unit tests. Hopefully you or your agents might find it useful.
